title: Distinguish moral distress responsibility and the support needed

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Moral distress can include guilt, betrayal and uncertainty about responsibility. A story alone cannot establish a diagnosis or legal liability. Clarify what was known, what authority existed and which kind of support can answer which question.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Fictional coordinator Ari allocates an ordinary access slot using the current list. A supervisor withheld a corrected eligibility note; Ari learned this only after Jo missed the slot. Ari had no access to that note beforehand and may request an independent process review, but cannot promise compensation. Jo permits a written acknowledgment, not a personal visit. Ari reports continuing distress without a supplied clinical assessment.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Separate Ari’s action, knowledge, institutional omission and unknown consequences. Choose proportionate accountability and distinct support roles without diagnosing either person.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A friend says guilt proves a clinical disorder and orders a legal admission. Which authority has been exceeded?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Acknowledge the decision and known missed access, request review of the withheld information and respect Jo’s contact limit. Qualified mental-health support can address concerning distress; an appropriate independent adviser can examine institutional/legal responsibility; a willing trusted person can offer company. None automatically settles the others. Partial: choose support without acknowledging the impact. Incorrect: assign all blame or none before examining the process.
criteria: Knowledge and role limit the responsibility account
Known harm and unresolved questions both remain

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: The friend has no supplied basis to diagnose or decide legal responsibility. Retain the feeling, seek suitable qualified assessment or advice where needed, and do not turn reassurance into a binding determination.
